extracted.intended_audience: naturalists, taxonomists, and students of natural history
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and guiding principles for biological classification (the Natural System), explaining which characters to use or avoid, how to weigh aggregates of characters, the role of embryology, rudimentary structures, geography, and the genealogical (descent-based) basis of classification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural system is genealogical (descent-based) in arrangement
rubrics_metrics.description: The arrangement of groups within each class, in due subordination and relation to other groups, must be strictly genealogical in order to be natural; the natural system is genealogical in its arrangement, like a pedigree.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classifications should reflect community of descent (shared ancestry). Use branching/pedigree metaphors and group subordinate to group to show filiation; recognize that genealogical arrangement remains true even when degrees of modification differ. Example: represent affinities with branching diagrams rather than linear lists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer characters less concerned with special habits (non-adaptive characters)
rubrics_metrics.description: It may be given as a general rule, that the less any part of the organisation is concerned with special habits, the more important it becomes for classification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid placing weight on characters that are obviously adaptive to particular habits or environments. Favor internal or 'remote' organs (e.g., generative organs) over external features directly tied to lifestyle. Example: Owen regarded generative organs of the dugong as revealing true affinities.

rubrics_metrics.name: High classificatory value of reproductive/generative organs (plants and animals)
rubrics_metrics.description: Organs of reproduction (generative organs in animals, organs of reproduction and seeds in plants) are of paramount importance in classification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In plants, embryonic leaves (cotyledons) and early development modes are used to define major divisions. In animals, generative organs may be less modified by habit and therefore reveal affinity. Use these where available as primary characters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use characters that are constant and widespread within group
rubrics_metrics.description: If a character is nearly uniform and common to a great number of forms, and not common to others, it is used as one of high value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize characters that persist across many species in a group even if their physiological importance seems small. The constancy across diverse habits is the key sign of value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rudimentary or atrophied organs often valuable for classification
rubrics_metrics.description: Rudimentary or atrophied organs, though of little physiological importance, are often of high value in exhibiting close affinities between groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use vestigial structures (e.g., rudimentary teeth or bones, rudimentary florets) as important classificatory evidence because their presence across taxa indicates inheritance from a common ancestor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Small or 'trifling' characters can be highly informative when correlated
rubrics_metrics.description: Numerous instances exist of characters derived from parts of very trifling physiological importance which are highly serviceable in defining whole groups (e.g., passage from nostrils to mouth, inflection of jaw angle, manner insect wings are folded).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not dismiss minor characters; their aggregate correlation with other characters across taxa can reveal descent. Examples include dermal covering (hair vs feathers) or wing-folding in insects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of an aggregate (correlated) characters over single characters
rubrics_metrics.description: The importance of an aggregate of characters is very evident: a species may depart from its allies in several important characters yet still be placed with them if an aggregate of other characters betrays common descent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rely on multiple correlated characters rather than any single trait. Classification founded on one character 'has always failed.' Seek combinations of traits even if each is slight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid classification based solely on single characters
rubrics_metrics.description: A classification founded on any single character, however important that may be, has always failed; no part of the organisation is universally constant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not elevate one organ or feature to sole determinant of group boundaries. Reassess groups when further species reveal intermediate states.

rubrics_metrics.name: Embryological characters carry high classificatory importance
rubrics_metrics.description: The structure of the embryo should often be of equal or superior importance to the adult for classification; embryonic characters have been strongly urged as the most important in classification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use embryology (developmental patterns, cotyledon number/position, plumule/radicle development, early ontogeny) to infer homologies and ancestry because early traits are less likely to have been modified by later adaptations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographical distribution can aid classification (especially in large groups)
rubrics_metrics.description: Geographical distribution has often been used, though perhaps not quite logically, in classification, especially in very large groups of closely allied forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use geographic patterns as supplementary evidence: species of the same genus in a distinct isolated region have likely descended from the same parents. But treat geography as an aid, not primary proof of affinity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish real affinities from analogical (adaptive) resemblances
rubrics_metrics.description: Analogical or adaptive characters (resemblances due to similar habits/environments) are of little value to the systematist and tend to conceal true blood-relationships.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify whether similarity results from common descent or parallel adaptation. Examples: dugong/whale/fish body shape is analogical; cetacean similarities within the whale family are true affinities because many shared characters indicate common ancestry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chains of affinities matter: intermediate links justify grouping extremes
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if two extreme forms share no common character, if they are connected by intermediate groups in a chain of affinities, they may be inferred to have common descent and be placed in the same class.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize and use transitional or intermediate taxa to justify placing morphologically divergent forms together (the chain concept). This explains classification in groups like crustaceans where no single character spans extremes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taxonomic ranks express degree of modification and are somewhat arbitrary
rubrics_metrics.description: Comparative value of groups such as orders, families, genera seems almost arbitrary; degree of difference among allied forms may lead to raising or lowering group rank as new species are found.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand that ranks (genus, family, etc.) are practical labels to express varying degrees of modification from common ancestors. Expect reclassification as additional taxa are discovered; do not treat ranks as absolute metaphysical categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classify varieties using the most constant characters (prefer natural over artificial groupings)
rubrics_metrics.description: In classing varieties, use the parts found to be most constant (e.g., horns in cattle) rather than the most important parts for utility (e.g., edible stems of turnips). If a real pedigree existed, genealogical classification would be preferred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For domestic or intraspecific variation, choose stable traits for grouping; avoid artificial systems that group by single economically important characters. Example: tumblers kept together because of common habit even when beak length differs.
